Two Routines, Not a Chain: Conﬁrmation Hearing
Opposition and the Allocation of Audit Scrutiny in the
Korean National Assembly
KNA Research Agents (AI-generated)
Experimental Output - kna-research-agents.com
August 24, 2026

Abstract
Legislators who publicly oppose a ministerial nominee at a conﬁrmation hearing might be
expected to scrutinize that ministry more intensively afterward. Position-taking accounts of
legislative oversight predict such carry-over; accounts of conﬁrmation hearings as party theater predict none. I adjudicate these opposing predictions with a pre-registered difference-indifferences design that links 7.4 million committee question-and-answer dyads from the Korean National Assembly to hand-coded hearing rosters and party-based opposition status for
three cohorts of ministerial nominees, with a speech-based coding of individually expressed
opposition as a robustness check. Opposing a nominee does not raise the conﬁrmed ministry’s
share of a legislator’s questions at the following annual state audit. The estimate is statistically
equivalent to zero at the threshold declared before estimation, placebo agencies move identically, an apparent baseline attention gap dissolves under committee ﬁxed effects, and a withinopposition intensity slope, which the achievable sample cannot resolve, is bounded below half
the pre-set bar. Conﬁrmation conﬂict and audit allocation appear to be separate institutional
routines rather than links in a causal chain.

Keywords: legislative oversight, conﬁrmation hearings, parliamentary questions, equivalence testing, South Korea

1

Introduction

Legislatures oversee the executive through a sequence of distinct institutional venues (??). They
screen the personnel who will lead ministries, and they later scrutinize what those ministries do.
An assumption connecting the two venues runs through both scholarship and institutional reform
debate: the conﬂict generated when a nominee is screened should reverberate through the scrutiny
that follows, because the legislators who fought the appointment acquired a stake in the ministry
they failed to keep out of the nominee’s hands. The assumption is consequential. In South Korea,
recurring proposals to reorganize the National Assembly’s conﬁrmation hearing system, including
proposals to divide the hearing into separate policy and ethics tracks, rest in part on beliefs about
what the hearing contributes to the Assembly’s subsequent oversight of the ministry (Choi et al.
2008; Yoon, Kim and Kang 2020). Whether conﬁrmation conﬂict in fact carries into later oversight
behavior, however, has not been established in any national setting.
Two literatures make opposite predictions about this carry-over, and they make them about the
same measurable quantity. The ﬁrst extends the study of confrontation in legislative oversight. Eldes, Fong and Lowande (2023) show that congressional oversight hearings mix information gathering with confrontation and that confrontation tracks partisan alignment with the administration.
If confrontation at a conﬁrmation hearing is individual position taking with reputational returns

(?), then a legislator who staked a public position against a nominee has invested in that ministry’s failure. Position-taking continuity predicts that the investment pays dividends in attention:
the conﬁrmed ministry should command a larger share of that legislator’s oversight questions after
the hearing than before. The second literature is the Korean scholarship on conﬁrmation hearings,
which has consistently characterized hearing behavior as an expression of executive-legislative
and partisan relations rather than of individual conviction (Choi et al. 2008; Jeon 2018; Yoon, Kim
and Kang 2020). On this account, opposing a nominee is a party-assigned role for the hearing day.
The role is discharged when the hearing adjourns, and the legislator’s oversight portfolio reverts to
the jurisdiction of the standing committee. Continuity predicts a positive shift in attention toward
the contested ministry; the party-theater account predicts none.
Despite mature literatures on conﬁrmation politics, on parliamentary questioning, and on legislative oversight, there exists, to my knowledge, no study in any country that tests whether the
positions legislators take at conﬁrmation hearings carry into those same legislators’ subsequent
oversight behavior. The fragments sit in three separate bodies of work that have not been connected. Conﬁrmation studies ask why nominees pass or fail (Yoon, Kim and Kang 2020). Oversight
studies ask how legislators behave once a hearing is under way (Eldes, Fong and Lowande 2023).
The parliamentary questions literature asks how parties allocate scrutiny across issues (?Senninger
2017). None follows the individual legislator across the boundary between the appointment ﬁght
and the oversight venue that comes after it. The gap matters because the two theoretical traditions
that could ﬁll it disagree, and because a reform debate proceeds as though the answer were known.
This article closes the gap with data from the Korean National Assembly, a setting unusually
well suited to the test. Ministerial nominees face mandatory conﬁrmation hearings before the
1

standing committee that holds jurisdiction over their ministry. Every autumn, the same standing committees conduct the state audit, a calendar-ﬁxed burst of police-patrol oversight in the
sense of ?, in which legislators question ministries and agencies directly; the audit falls ﬁve to
ten months after the spring and early-summer hearing cohorts within the Assembly’s rigid institutional time structure (Ka 2025). Because the same legislators question the same ministries in
consecutive audits, the design can compare each legislator’s allocation of audit attention before
and after the hearing at which the legislator took a position on the nominee. I draw on a corpus of
9.9 million committee speech acts and 7.4 million question-and-answer dyads spanning the 16th
through 22nd Assemblies, hand-code hearing rosters and party-based opposition status for three
cohorts of ministerial nominees heard in 2020 to 2021, 2022, and 2023, and estimate a difference-indifferences model of the conﬁrmed ministry’s share of each legislator’s audit questions; a second
coding drawn from each legislator’s own hearing speech probes the individually expressed construct. The primary threshold, a shift of ﬁve percentage points, and the falsiﬁcation criteria were
declared before estimation, following the logic of arguing for a negligible effect (Rainey 2014), and
the placebo machinery follows the equivalence approach of Hartman and Hidalgo (2018).
The answer is a null at the margin the design was built to measure, and a bound at the one
margin it cannot resolve. Legislators who opposed a nominee do not shift their audit questioning toward the conﬁrmed ministry. The estimated change is small, statistically indistinguishable
from zero, and formally equivalent to zero at the pre-registered threshold; the minimum detectable
effect binds well below that threshold, so an effect of the size the continuity hypothesis predicts
would have been detected with at least 80 percent probability. Placebo agencies, which no nominee
headed, move identically, and the placebo estimate is equivalent to zero at even half the registered
margin. An apparent baseline gap, in which opposed legislators already devoted more of their
audit questions to the ministry before the hearing, dissolves under committee ﬁxed effects: it reﬂects the composition of committee jurisdictions, driven almost entirely by one committee whose
witness list is effectively a single ministry. Within opposition questioners, the intensity of hearing
engagement is associated with a positive but small reallocation that the achievable sample cannot
resolve; that margin is reported as inconclusive within a pre-set bound, with the conﬁdence bound
sitting below half the bar for a diluted continuity effect. A separate cohort of nominees whose
hearings spanned a full change of government between audits shows the same null, suggesting
the result is not an artifact of one partisan conﬁguration.
The article makes four contributions. Empirically, it adjudicates a contradiction between two
literatures and ﬁnds that neither positive mechanism operates at the individual level: audit allocation follows committee jurisdiction, and conﬁrmation conﬂict leaves no measurable trace on it.
This narrows the scope of position-taking continuity arguments and disciplines the party-theater
reading, which had itself predicted a baseline attention pattern that the data attribute to composition. Methodologically, it offers a template for informative null results in legislative studies:
pre-registered thresholds, binding minimum detectable effects, formal equivalence tests, and two
self-corrections executed by pre-committed decision rules rather than post hoc judgment. For in-

2

stitutional reform, the Korean debate over restructuring conﬁrmation hearings has assumed that
hearing conﬂict has an oversight externality at the audit; the evidence here bounds that externality,
equivalent to zero at the pre-registered threshold at the main margin and conﬁned below half the
pre-set bar at the intensity margin the design cannot fully resolve. On scope, ﬁnally, the article
documents the limits of the claim with care: the attention literature predicts that confrontationgenerated attention decays within weeks to months (Birkland 1998; Walgrave, Soroka and Nuytemans 2007; Vliegenthart et al. 2016), so a short-range carry-over could exist and be fully discharged
before October; the test here concerns the audit, the venue the carry-over claim itself names.
The next section derives the competing hypotheses and pre-registered thresholds from the
oversight, conﬁrmation, and political-attention literatures; the sections that follow describe the
data and identiﬁcation strategy, report the main estimates, equivalence tests, and secondary margins, and draw out the implications for theory and for the reform debate.

2

Literature and Theory

2.1

Position Taking and the Continuity of Confrontation

The study of legislative oversight long centered on institutional design, on the choice between
centralized patrols and decentralized alarms and on the committee structures that carry scrutiny

(??); recent work has moved toward legislator behavior within oversight venues. Eldes, Fong and
Lowande (2023) analyze congressional oversight hearings and distinguish two currents in member
questioning: the gathering of information and the staging of confrontation. Their central ﬁnding
is that confrontation is patterned by partisan alignment, with members of the party opposed to
the administration confronting witnesses at higher rates. The ﬁnding concerns behavior within
a single venue. The natural extension, and the ﬁrst theoretical position this article tests, is that
confrontation crosses venues: a member who confronts an administration ﬁgure in one setting
acquires commitments that shape behavior in later settings.
Continuity could arise through consistency pressure, through reputational investment, or through
the economics of expertise. Consistency pressure operates because a legislator who declared a
nominee unﬁt has issued a public prediction that the ministry will be led badly; subsequent scrutiny
of that ministry is the natural way to vindicate the prediction, and inattention would expose the
original opposition as costless talk. Reputational investment operates because opposition at a nationally televised hearing is a position-taking act in the classic sense of ?, and position taking generates returns only if audiences can connect the position to later behavior; a legislator known as
the nominee’s chief antagonist plausibly has a branded issue in that ministry’s performance. The
expertise mechanism is humbler: preparing to interrogate a nominee requires acquiring knowledge of the ministry’s programs and failures, and expertise lowers the cost of future questioning,
so once the ﬁxed cost is sunk, the marginal audit question directed at that ministry is cheap. All
three mechanisms point the same way. Extended to the appointment context, they predict that a
legislator who opposed a conﬁrmed nominee should allocate a durably larger share of oversight
3

attention to the conﬁrmed ministry than the legislator did before the hearing.

2.2

Conﬁrmation Hearings as Party Theater

The Korean literature on conﬁrmation hearings supports a different reading of what hearing opposition is. Content analyses of prime ministerial hearings ﬁnd that questioning tracks the state
of executive-legislative relations rather than the properties of individual nominees, with hearings
functioning as a stage on which the standing conﬂict between government and opposition is performed (Choi et al. 2008). Topic-model analyses of hearing transcripts reach a compatible conclusion: the discourse of the hearing is structured by the government-assembly relationship of the
moment (Jeon 2018). Studies of conﬁrmation outcomes ﬁnd that approval and rejection are driven
by the partisan conﬁguration surrounding the nomination rather than by nominee quality as such

(Yoon, Kim and Kang 2020). Across these studies the individual legislator appears as the bearer of
a party role. Opposition to the nominee is assigned, performed for the hearing day, and discharged
when the hearing adjourns.
If hearing opposition is a discharged role, it should leave no residue in the legislator’s subsequent behavior. The audit is governed by a different routine: committee jurisdiction determines
which ministries a legislator can question, party strategy determines the topics of the season, and
the individual position taken months earlier at a hearing determines nothing. The comparative
literature on parliamentary questions reinforces this expectation from a different direction (?). Opposition parties use questions for selective scrutiny tied to the strategic issue opportunities of the
moment, not to standing grudges (Senninger 2017). Question agendas respond to media attention and focusing events, and the response is concentrated in the immediate window (Walgrave,
Soroka and Nuytemans 2007; Vliegenthart et al. 2016). Nothing in this literature suggests that a
months-old appointment ﬁght should organize a legislator’s question allocation at the next audit.

2.3

Attention Dynamics and the Audit Calendar

The timing structure of the Korean case disciplines what either theory can claim. The state audit is
not a continuous oversight channel; it is a calendar-ﬁxed annual burst embedded in the National
Assembly’s rigid institutional time structure, in which ﬁxed session windows govern when legislative attention can be spent at all (Ka 2025). Ministerial hearing cohorts concentrate in spring
and early summer, so the audit arrives ﬁve to ten months after the typical hearing. The politicalattention literature speaks directly to what should survive such a gap. Media effects on parliamentary agendas operate at the weekly-to-monthly scale and dissipate quickly (Walgrave, Soroka and
Nuytemans 2007); pooled evidence from seven countries conﬁrms that media-to-questions transfer is strongest for opposition parties and concentrated in the immediate window (Vliegenthart
et al. 2016); and even major focusing events produce attention spikes that decay within months as
agendas revert to baseline (Birkland 1998).
The audit is therefore a demanding but fair venue for the continuity prediction. Demanding,

4

because the decay literature suggests any confrontation-generated attention could be fully discharged before October; fair, because the carry-over claim in the Korean reform debate names
the audit speciﬁcally, and the argument that hearings improve oversight presumes the improvement shows up where oversight institutionally happens. A further implication concerns the scope
of any ﬁnding. A null at the audit does not rule out carry-over at shorter range, for instance in
current-issues questioning during the weeks after appointment. The claim tested here is the claim
the debate makes, and the decay literature independently predicts that the ﬁve-to-ten-month gap
is long enough for full dissipation of short-lived attention effects.

2.4

Hypotheses and Pre-Registered Thresholds

The two theoretical positions yield predictions about a single quantity: the change, from the audit
before the hearing to the audit after it, in the share of a legislator’s audit questions directed at the
conﬁrmed ministry, compared between legislators who opposed and legislators who supported
the nominee.
H1 (position-taking continuity). Legislators who opposed a conﬁrmed nominee increase the conﬁrmed ministry’s share of their audit questions relative to supportive
legislators on the same committee. The pre-registered threshold for a substantively
meaningful effect is ﬁve percentage points.
H2 (party theater). The difference-in-differences lies within the pre-registered equivalence margin of zero. Audit allocation reverts to committee jurisdiction and party role
once the hearing ends.
Two secondary margins were speciﬁed in advance, each with its own decision rule ﬁxed before
estimation. The intensity margin asks whether continuity, if diluted by pooling all opposed legislators, surfaces among those who engaged the nominee most heavily: within opposition questioners, a one-standard-deviation increase in hearing engagement, measured as the count of question
dyads the legislator directed at the nominee and standardized within committee, must raise the
difference-in-differences outcome by at least 2.5 percentage points, half the original threshold, for
continuity to survive in diluted form. The levels margin arose from early analysis, in which opposed legislators appeared to devote more of their audit questions to the ministry already before
the hearing, a pattern initially read as favoring the party-theater account, since it suggests opposition assignment and ministry attention are parallel expressions of the same party role. The precommitted rule stated that this levels gap would count as a ﬁnding only if it survived committee
ﬁxed effects; if it collapsed, it would be reported as composition and dropped from the adjudication. Both rules were honored, and the second ﬁred against the project’s own earlier reading, as
the Results section reports.
Finally, the design commits to the standards of the negligible-effect literature. A null claim is
informative only against an explicitly declared magnitude, demonstrated by conﬁdence intervals
5

that exclude effects larger than the declared threshold (Rainey 2014), and placebo claims should
be stated as equivalence results rather than as failures to reject (Hartman and Hidalgo 2018). The
ﬁve-percentage-point threshold, the 2.5-point diluted bar, and the placebo margins reported below
were all ﬁxed before the corresponding estimates were computed.

3

Data and Method

3.1

Data

The analysis draws on the hearings module of the Korean National Assembly (KNA) database,
a corpus of committee transcripts spanning the 16th through 22nd Assemblies that contains 9.9
million individual speech acts and 7.4 million question-and-answer dyads linking a questioning
legislator to an answering witness. Within this corpus I identify, for each ministerial conﬁrmation
hearing, the set of legislators who questioned the nominee, and I follow those same legislators into
the annual state audits immediately preceding and immediately following the hearing. The unit
of analysis is the legislator-ministry pair: a legislator who questioned a nominee for a given ministry, observed in both the pre-hearing and post-hearing audits of the standing committee holding
jurisdiction over that ministry.
Three cohorts of ministerial nominees enter the analysis. Cohort 1 comprises nominees heard
in 2020 and 2021, with the audits of October 2020 and October 2021 as the pre- and post-periods.
Cohort 2 comprises nominees heard in 2023, bracketed by the audits of 2022 and 2023. Cohorts 1
and 2 together constitute the pooled pre-registered sample of 278 legislator-ministry pairs across
191 legislators. Cohort 3 comprises the nominees of May 2022, whose pre- and post-audits span the
transfer of power from the Moon administration to the Yoon administration; because the governing
status of every party ﬂips between its two audits, this cohort serves as an out-of-sample consistency
check under a full change of government rather than as part of the pooled test. Table 1 summarizes
the samples.
Treatment. A legislator-ministry pair is coded opposed when the legislator questioned the nominee and belonged, at the hearing date, to a party opposed to the nominating president; pairs of
legislators from the president’s party are coded supportive. The construct this primary coding
measures deserves explicit statement. Party-based opposition status captures the assigned opposition role at the hearing, not an individually expressed position, so it tests the party-theater account
on its own terms while testing the individual position taking that H1 invokes only indirectly. The
analysis therefore also codes opposition directly from the legislator’s own hearing speech, classifying a legislator as opposed when the legislator called for the nominee’s withdrawal or declared
the nominee unﬁt; this speech-based coding is the construct-faithful measure of individually expressed opposition, and it is reported alongside the primary speciﬁcation in the robustness analysis, where it returns the same null. Hearing rosters were hand-coded before any outcome analysis,
with 400 member entries for cohorts 1 and 2 and 325 for cohort 3 written to append-only dictionaries. Two coding hazards deserve note because both were caught by internal checks. The ﬁrst

concerns party labels: the corpus records each legislator’s party as a term-start snapshot, so members of parties that renamed or merged mid-term carry outdated labels; coding governing status
from raw labels inverts 88 of 97 codings in one cohort, and all analyses therefore recode party by
the nominating president’s party at the speech date, predecessor labels included. The second concerns identity: a name-keyed merge contaminated one supportive-side observation because the
21st Assembly seats two legislators who share a name; all merges in the replication package key
on unique member identiﬁers with a uniqueness assertion, and the corrected merge leaves every
headline quantity unchanged at reporting precision.
Outcome. The outcome is the conﬁrmed ministry’s share of the legislator’s question dyads at
the state audit, differenced between the post- and pre-hearing audits and expressed in percentage
points. The placebo outcome applies the same construction to named government agencies that
no nominee in the cohort headed; if opposed legislators simply become more active questioners of
government witnesses in general, the placebo moves with the main outcome, whereas a ministrydirected carry-over moves only the main outcome. The intensity measure, used in the withinopposition dose test, is the total count of hearing question dyads the legislator directed at the
ministry’s nominee or nominees, standardized within committee because hearing length varies
mechanically across committees.
Reproducibility. The full pipeline reruns end to end deterministically: all persisted artifacts reproduce byte-identically, and the hand-coded dictionaries reproduce the analysis samples exactly
on the unique-identiﬁer key. All estimates reported below were regenerated in the ﬁnal consolidation run rather than transcribed from earlier analyses.
7

3.2

Identiﬁcation Strategy

The primary speciﬁcation is a difference-in-differences model estimated in changes. For legislator

i questioning ministry m under the jurisdiction of committee c,
∆Yim = β1 Opposedim + δc(i,m) + ϵim ,

(1 )

where ∆Yim is the change in ministry m’s share of legislator i’s audit questions from the prehearing to the post-hearing audit, Opposedim indicates hearing opposition, and δc(i,m) are committee ﬁxed effects. Standard errors are clustered by legislator throughout. Because the model is
estimated in changes, any time-invariant difference between opposed and supportive legislators
in their level of attention to the ministry is removed by construction; the committee ﬁxed effects
additionally absorb jurisdiction-speciﬁc shifts in audit agendas between the two years. The withinopposition dose test replaces the treatment indicator with the standardized engagement measure,

∆Yim = β2 Doseim + δc(i,m) + ϵim ,

(2 )

estimated on opposition questioners only.
Four threats to inference structure the design. Nonrandom assignment comes ﬁrst: opposition
is not randomly assigned but follows party. Nonrandom assignment, however, is not a nuisance
but part of the estimand: the question is whether the opposition role, however assigned, generates
individual carry-over, and the changes speciﬁcation compares opposed and supportive members
of the same committee across the same pair of audits. The identifying assumption is parallel trends
in ministry shares absent the hearing, and the placebo-agency outcome provides a direct check,
since any committee-wide or party-wide trend in questioning activity should appear there as well.
Differential attrition is the second threat: selective exit could distort the sample of pairs observed
in both audits, but retention is closely balanced, at 0.864 for opposed and 0.832 for supportive
pairs. Mechanical composition is the third, because composition can masquerade as behavior:
in committees whose audit witness list is dominated by a single ministry, the share outcome is
pinned near its ceiling, and one such committee, the Gender Equality and Family Committee, has a
mean pre-period share of 0.963; the levels analysis below shows how this cell alone manufactured
an apparent attention gap. Power is the fourth, since the informativeness of a null depends on
it. The pooled design’s minimum detectable effect at 80 percent power is 3.1 percentage points,
comfortably below the pre-registered ﬁve-point threshold, so the design binds: an effect of the size
the continuity hypothesis predicts would have been detected with at least 80 percent probability.
Following Rainey (2014), the null claim is stated against the declared threshold, and following
Hartman and Hidalgo (2018), placebo and main estimates are additionally subjected to two-onesided equivalence tests at pre-speciﬁed margins.
The dose test carries one further caveat that no speciﬁcation can remove. Legislators who question a nominee intensively may be the committee’s pre-existing specialists in that ministry, so the
dose partly proxies standing portfolio interest rather than hearing-generated animus. The changes
8

speciﬁcation absorbs the level of specialization but not differential trends among specialists. For
this reason, and because the achievable opposition sample cannot resolve effects of the observed
magnitude, the dose result is reported as a bound rather than as a ﬁnding.

The pooled estimate is a decline of 0.9 percentage points in the conﬁrmed ministry’s share, with
a 95 percent conﬁdence interval running from roughly −3.0 to +1.3 percentage points (Table 2,
column 1). Nothing in a legislator’s audit allocation shifts toward the ministry whose nominee the
legislator opposed. The estimate is not merely non-signiﬁcant; it is signed against the continuity
prediction, and the design’s minimum detectable effect of 3.1 percentage points binds well below
the pre-registered ﬁve-point threshold, so the pre-set falsiﬁcation condition for H1 is met. The
cohort-level estimates in columns 2 and 3 are individually consistent with the pooled null, and the
government-change cohort in column 4 is null as well: even when the opposed legislators moved
from governing party to opposition between their two audits, their allocation toward the contested
ministry did not move. The placebo estimate in column 5 is the most instructive single number
in the table. Its point estimate differs from the main estimate by less than 0.01 percentage points,
indicating that whatever small common drift exists in questioning activity is wholly generic rather
than directed at the conﬁrmed ministry.

4.2

Equivalence Tests

A null result is informative only if the data afﬁrmatively rule out effects of the declared size (Rainey
2014). Figure 2 presents the two-one-sided equivalence tests, plotting the 90 percent conﬁdence
intervals for the main and placebo estimates against the pre-registered ﬁve-point margin and the
stricter 2.5-point margin.
The results are asymmetric by design, and the asymmetry should be stated exactly. The placebo
estimate is formally equivalent to zero within plus or minus 2.5 percentage points: its 90 percent
interval sits entirely inside even the half-registered margin, which converts the informal claim
that placebo agencies move identically into the afﬁrmative equivalence statement that Hartman
and Hidalgo (2018) recommend. The main estimate is formally equivalent to zero within the preregistered ﬁve-point margin, but not within the stricter 2.5-point margin, because its lower bound
extends slightly past that line. The correct summary is therefore that the effect of hearing opposition is bounded below the substantive threshold declared before estimation, while the placebo is

equivalent to zero at even half that threshold. Claiming the stricter equivalence for the main effect
would overstate the evidence, and the paper does not.

The null survives every variation. Coding opposition from what legislators actually said at
the hearing, the construct-faithful measure of individually expressed position taking, rather than
from the party they belonged to, leaves the estimate negative and indistinguishable from zero (Table 3, column 1). Replacing the share outcome with the log count of questions directed at the
11

ministry, which guards against the possibility that shares conceal offsetting movements in overall
questioning volume, produces the same conclusion (column 2), as does restricting the denominator to questions aimed at named agencies (column 3). No speciﬁcation in Table 2 or Table 3
produces a positive estimate that approaches conventional signiﬁcance, and none approaches the
pre-registered threshold.

4.4

The Levels Margin: An Apparent Gap Dissolves

An earlier stage of this project identiﬁed what looked like the arc’s one positive ﬁnding: in the
raw cohort-1 data, opposed legislators already devoted 4.6 percentage points more of their audit
questions to the ministry than supportive legislators did before the hearing ever took place. That
pattern was initially read as evidence for the party-theater account, on the logic that opposition
assignment and ministry-directed attention are parallel expressions of the same party role. The precommitted decision rule stated that the gap would count as a ﬁnding only if it survived committee
ﬁxed effects. Table 4 reports the test.

The gap does not survive. Holding committee constant, the cohort-1 estimate collapses from
4.6 percentage points to well under one point, with a conﬁdence interval straddling zero (Table 4,
column 1). The decomposition identiﬁes the source precisely: one committee does nearly all the
work. In the Gender Equality and Family Committee, the conﬁrmed ministry is effectively the
entire audit witness list, so every member’s share sits near its ceiling, and seven of the committee’s
11 pairs happen to be opposed; dropping that single cell reduces the raw gap by roughly seveneighths. The pooled residual in column 2 is marginal, and column 3 shows why it cannot be read as
ministry-directed attention: opposed legislators exhibit a same-signed and larger gap on placebo
agencies that no nominee headed. What little remains is the generic pattern that opposition members direct more questions at named government witnesses of every kind. The pre-committed
rule therefore ﬁred: the levels register drops from the adjudication, and the simplest description
the data license is that the level of audit attention follows committee jurisdiction.

4.5

The Intensity Margin: A Bounded Residual

The ﬁnal margin on which the continuity hypothesis could survive is intensity. If carry-over exists
but is diluted by pooling every opposed legislator, it should concentrate among those who engaged
the nominee most heavily. Table 5 reports the within-opposition dose speciﬁcations of Equation 2,
and Figure 3 displays them against the pre-set diluted-continuity bar of 2.5 percentage points per
standard deviation.

13

The dose results land between the two theories, and the honest classiﬁcation is a bound. Every
speciﬁcation returns a positive slope, and the placebo slope in column 5 is centered on zero, so
whatever tilt exists does not appear on agencies the hearings did not touch. Yet no point estimate
reaches the pre-set diluted-continuity bar, and only one of six speciﬁcations, the log-dose variant,
excludes zero, a pattern consistent with fragility rather than signal. Neither pre-registered decision
rule can ﬁre: the survival bar of 2.5 points per standard deviation is not met by any point estimate,
while the failure condition, an interval excluding that bar on a sample of at least 150 opposition
pairs, cannot ﬁre at the achievable 138. The design’s minimum detectable effect on this sample
is roughly two percentage points per standard deviation, so an effect of the observed magnitude
is unresolvable by construction. What the data support is the bounding statement: at 95 percent
conﬁdence, the within-opposition intensity slope lies below 2.7 percentage points per standard
deviation of hearing engagement (Table 5, column 1), below half the original threshold. The continuity hypothesis is weakened at this margin, not killed, and the specialization confound discussed
above gives an additional reason not to promote the residual tilt to a ﬁnding.

4.6

Summary of Results

Across 18 pre-committed tests and robustness checks, the pattern is uniform. The pre-registered
carry-over prediction fails with a binding minimum detectable effect and a placebo that moves
identically; the null is formally equivalent to zero at the registered margin; it holds under an alternative treatment coding, alternative outcomes, and a full change of government; the one apparent
positive ﬁnding dissolves into committee composition under a pre-committed rule; and the intensity margin is inconclusive rather than resolved, bounded below half the declared threshold.
Audit attention, in levels and in changes, tracks committee jurisdiction.

5

Discussion

Two literatures made opposite predictions for the same quantity, and the data adjudicate cleanly.
Position-taking continuity, extended from ? through the confrontation-in-oversight work of Eldes, Fong and Lowande (2023), predicted that a legislator who staked a public position against
a nominee acquires a durable stake in that ministry’s failure, raising the ministry’s share of the
legislator’s questions at the following state audit. The Korean conﬁrmation-hearing literature predicted instead that hearing opposition is a party-assigned role for the hearing day, discharged
when the hearing ends, with audit allocation reverting to committee jurisdiction (Choi et al. 2008;
Jeon 2018; Yoon, Kim and Kang 2020). The continuity prediction fails at the party level, with an
estimate equivalent to zero at the threshold declared before estimation, and it fails again under a
full change of government between audits. Within opposition questioners, the intensity margin is
bounded below half the pre-set bar. What the levels of audit attention track is neither hearing opposition nor its intensity but committee jurisdiction: the apparent baseline gap between opposed and
supportive legislators dissolves under committee ﬁxed effects and is matched by a larger placebo
14

gap. Conﬁrmation conﬂict and audit allocation appear to be two separate institutional routines,
not a causal chain.
The adjudication is narrower than a simple victory for the party-theater account, and the narrowing deserves emphasis. The zero-change prediction of the party-theater reading held, but the
reading had also seemed to gain support from the baseline levels pattern, and that support is now
gone: the levels evidence turned out to discriminate for nothing except the composition of committee witness lists. The description the data license is more austere than either theory. Allocation
follows jurisdiction. Party assignment may well govern who performs opposition at the hearing,
as the Korean literature documents, but the performance leaves no measurable residue in the performer’s subsequent allocation of oversight attention, and the party role does not even generate
the standing attention premium that a strong role-based account might expect.
The results align well with what the political-attention literature would predict for this venue.
Attention transfer into parliamentary questions is fast and short-lived, operating at the weekly-tomonthly scale (Walgrave, Soroka and Nuytemans 2007; Vliegenthart et al. 2016), and even major
focusing events produce spikes that revert within months (Birkland 1998). The state audit sits ﬁve
to ten months downstream of the typical hearing, inside a calendar that ﬁxes when oversight attention can be spent at all (Ka 2025). A carry-over effect could in principle exist at shorter range,
in current-issues questioning during the weeks after appointment, and be fully discharged by October. This study does not test that channel, and the null here does not speak to it. What the study
shows is that conﬁrmation conﬂict does not carry into the audit, the oversight venue where the
Korean reform debate has assumed the hearing’s externality lands. The scope statement and the
venue were both ﬁxed by the prior being tested, not chosen after the fact.
The results also reﬁne, rather than contradict, the confrontation ﬁndings that motivated the
continuity hypothesis. Eldes, Fong and Lowande (2023) document that partisanship shapes the
style of oversight questioning, with opposition-aligned members confronting witnesses at higher
rates. Nothing here disputes that. The government-change cohort is instructive on exactly this
point: when the opposed legislators’ party moved from governing to opposition between the two
audits, a shift that should transform confrontation incentives, their allocation of questions across
ministries still did not move. Partisan alignment appears to govern how legislators question, while
jurisdiction governs whom they question; the appointment ﬁght changes neither. The ﬁnding
similarly complements Senninger (2017): opposition scrutiny follows the strategic opportunities
of the moment, and a months-old hearing position does not seem to constitute one.
Several limitations bound these conclusions, and they should be stated plainly. The outcome
is allocation, not content: legislators who opposed a nominee might question the conﬁrmed ministry no more often but more aggressively, and a tone-based or confrontation-coded outcome could
in principle detect a carry-over that share-based allocation misses; that channel remains untested
here. The intensity margin is unresolved rather than resolved: the dose slope is positive in every speciﬁcation and clean on placebo agencies, but the achievable opposition sample cannot distinguish an effect of the observed size from zero, and the specialization confound means even a

15

resolved positive slope would not identify hearing-generated attention, so the bound reported is
the honest object. Treatment is observational, and the primary coding is party-based: opposition
follows party, the party-based indicator captures the assigned role rather than an individually
expressed position, and although the changes speciﬁcation, committee ﬁxed effects, placebo outcomes, balanced retention, and the speech-based robustness coding address the sharpest threats,
no design element delivers the counterfactual of a randomly assigned hearing antagonist. Some
cells are thin: the cohort-2 supportive side contributes 26 pairs, and single-ministry committees
are unusable for share outcomes, a design lesson this study learned by initially mistaking one
such committee’s composition for behavior. The setting, ﬁnally, is one country with a distinctive
oversight calendar: the tight coupling of hearings and audits to the same standing committees is
what makes the test possible, but it also means the decay window between conﬂict and oversight
opportunity is institutionally ﬁxed at ﬁve to ten months, and systems with continuous questioning
channels might show short-range dynamics this design cannot observe.
Finally, the trajectory of the project is part of the evidence, and it is reported as procedure
rather than confession. Two ﬁndings were overturned by pre-committed decision rules during
the research: the original carry-over prior fell to its pre-registered falsiﬁer, and the baseline levels
gap, at one stage the project’s candidate positive ﬁnding, fell to the ﬁxed-effects rule that had been
attached to it in advance. Both retreats were logged when they occurred, and neither headline
claim depends on any result that failed its own pre-set test. In the framework of Rainey (2014),
the value of a null rests on declared magnitudes and demonstrated power; in this study it rests
additionally on decision rules that ﬁred against the analysts’ own earlier readings, which may be
the more demanding certiﬁcation.

6

Conclusion

This article asked whether the conﬂict legislators stage over ministerial appointments carries into
their subsequent oversight of the ministries those appointments ﬁll. Adjudicating between a positiontaking continuity extension of the oversight literature and the party-theater reading of Korean
conﬁrmation hearings, I linked hand-coded hearing rosters and party-based opposition status for
three nominee cohorts, supplemented by a speech-based coding of individually expressed opposition, to 7.4 million question-and-answer dyads from the Korean National Assembly and estimated
a pre-registered difference-in-differences model of audit question allocation. The answer is a null
with unusually complete credentials: equivalent to zero at the threshold declared before estimation, placebo-veriﬁed in the formal equivalence sense, robust to alternative treatment codings and
outcomes, stable across a change of government, and accompanied by a bounded intensity residual and a dissolved levels gap. Audit attention follows committee jurisdiction; the appointment
ﬁght leaves no measurable trace on it.
The contribution is threefold. Theoretically, the ﬁnding sets a scope condition on positiontaking continuity: whatever stakes a conﬁrmation ﬁght creates do not survive the ﬁve-to-ten-

16

month passage to the next audit, consistent with the fast decay the attention literature documents.
For the study of the Korean National Assembly, the ﬁnding replaces an assumed linkage between
two prominent oversight institutions with a measured absence of one. For institutional reform,
the implication is direct: proposals to restructure conﬁrmation hearings should not be premised
on an oversight externality at the audit, because the carry-over such proposals presume is equivalent to zero at the threshold declared before estimation, and the residual intensity slope, which
the design cannot fully resolve, is bounded below half that threshold. Conﬁrmation hearings may
serve screening, accountability, or position-taking functions on their own terms; improving later
audit scrutiny does not appear to be among them.
Future research should pursue the two channels this design could not reach. The ﬁrst is shortrange carry-over, in current-issues questioning during the weeks immediately after appointment,
where the attention literature predicts any effect would concentrate. The second is tone: whether
opposed legislators question the conﬁrmed ministry differently, if not more. Comparative extension to systems with continuous questioning channels would test whether the null reported here is
a property of appointment conﬂict generally or of calendars that separate conﬂict from oversight
opportunity by months. Each extension would beneﬁt from the same discipline this study relied
on: thresholds declared ﬁrst, and decision rules that are allowed to ﬁre against the researcher.
